results.note: Independently extracted AM pp. 8 and 21 and inspected the text at 150 dpi and Table 3 at 300 dpi. The no-strip column (n = 11) prints daily illicit opioid use 9 (81.8%) to 4 (36.4%), daily injection 4 (36.4%) to 2 (18.2%), and non-fatal overdose 2 to 0; none has a significance mark. Results 3.1 on AM p. 8 says the nonuser changes did not reach significance, likely because of the small sample. The at-least-one-strip column (n = 57) directly prints overdose 4 (7.0%) to 1 (1.8%). Counts and percentages independently recompute. The qualifying role and locators are appropriate. No correction.

Independently extracted the specified pages, inspected Methods at 150 dpi and Tables 3-4 at 300 dpi, and checked the printed ORs, CIs, category probabilities, Table 3 comparisons and notes. The two separate cumulative cutpoints give 3.640036731 and 5.285495079. Varying each relevant printed probability by 0.0005 gives endpoint ranges 3.391109420-3.918376653 and 5.260304612-5.310830687, reproducing the displayed three-decimal bounds; they are disjoint and exclude 19.918. For a common cumulative-logit model, inverse-linking a linear LSmean with identical covariate weights makes the positive-minus-negative link contrast the same at both cutpoints, so both odds ratios equal that model contrast. Averaging probabilities instead can yield different ratios, independently checked with a mathematical two-stratum example; that does not identify this study's procedure. The supplied paper describes the LSmean calculation but supplies no fitted model object or prediction code (and has no embedded files). It supports neither a replacement adjusted OR nor a corrected subgroup ranking. Baseline overdose is a covariate, no harm outcome is analysed, and the paper calls all presented p-values descriptive, including those other than the primary any-change association. The qualifying role is appropriate. No numerical correction.

Locator-only correction: add AM p. 22, where Table 3 note [dagger] explicitly identifies the n = 59 who reported opioid use at follow-up, and name Methods 2.2.2 on AM p. 5 for the contrasting drug-use recall windows. The extracted content and qualifying role are confirmed, with no numerical correction. Independently extracted the specified pages and the continuing Table 3 footnotes, and inspected text at 150 dpi and the figure/tables at 300 dpi. The paper's own one-month labels coexist with its reported average of 56 days and 22.1% within the one-month goal. Methods 2.2.4 gives past-month solitary use and overdose at both visits, while 2.2.2 gives six months versus one month for drug use. Independently, 99/103 = 96.1%, the completers' Table 1 baseline is 95.6%, and 56/59 = 94.9% with 40/59 = 67.8% at follow-up; thus the abstract's rounded 96% is not that paired baseline.
